title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: ~60 MB/cm^2 per sheet times 800 sheets is ~50 GB/cm^3, versus ~2 GB/cm^3 for a DIMM. Roll-to-roll costs (~$20-50/m^2 per sheet) keep cost per module flat; sheet alignment and yield are the risks.
note: If 800 laminated R2R TFT sheets yield, cost/GB falls >10x; sheet yield, alignment and through-stack interconnect are near-miraculous.

title: Minify $/m2 3000x: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted memory foil
idea: Run steel or polyimide foil webs through R2R UV-nanoimprint at ~100 nm half-pitch with sputtered IGZO channels and anodized-aluminum high-k capacitors, making 0.4 um2 gain cells on kilometers of foil, then laminate and slit into memory ribbons.
why: At ~$20-40/m2 processed and ~300 GB/m2 (~1/80 DRAM density), cost lands at ~$0.07-0.13/GB, about 100x cheaper, trading speed (~200 ns), refresh energy and module size.
note: Multilayer 100 nm overlay on flexible foil is the killer; if solved ~10x cost/bit for a slow tier.

title: Rail yard master: racetrack memory built in U.S. hard-disk head fabs
idea: A rail yard master moves cars along sidings instead of building a track for each car. Magnetic domain-wall racetrack memory uses vertical U-shaped nanowires, each holding ~64 domains shifted by current past one read/write head. It is built in U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs, which already pattern 20 nm magnetic multilayers in volume and are losing HDD demand.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 bits per ~4F^2 track footprint is ~10-20x DRAM areal density. The head fabs are depreciated, domain-wall motion does not wear out, and shift latency is tens of ns; pinning and shift errors are the risks.
note: Head-fab reuse is clever, but vertical racetrack has stalled for 15+ years on pinning and shift errors.

title: Open-hardware DRAM tester kits that issue signed grade certificates
idea: Learning from ham-radio networks, a 10-person company sells ~$300 FPGA tester kits with secure elements to e-waste recyclers worldwide. Each run produces a cryptographically signed certificate (pattern suite, retention, speed bin) bound to the module serial, so remote buyers can trust second-hand memory.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in secondary memory markets; signed provenance could unlock millions of modules a year.
note: Cheap signed-certificate testers address buyer distrust in used memory.

title: Eliminate software bloat: memory-footprint bounties for top open-source apps
idea: Eliminate wasted bytes: a $1M bounty fund pays per verified MB saved, times installed base, for merged patches that cut resident memory in Chromium, Electron, Firefox, Kubernetes components and JVM defaults, measured on a public benchmark.
why: A 10% cut in browser/Electron memory across billions of devices frees hundreds of PB of effective capacity and delays RAM upgrades.

title: Double-blind inventory clearinghouse to kill DRAM bullwhip hoarding
idea: Po: every warehouse is made of glass. A neutral party collects encrypted inventory and order data from DRAM makers, distributors and top buyers and, via secure multiparty computation, publishes only weekly aggregate true-demand and channel-inventory indices (like JODI for oil).
why: Double-ordering and hoarding amplify a ~10-15% supply gap into a 4x price spike; transparency deflates phantom demand and lets fabs plan capacity; attacks effective supply.
note: MPC aggregate indices are feasible; participation incentives are the real hurdle.

title: Eliminate test hardware: bootable signed DIMM health certificate
idea: Eliminate expensive ATE for used-memory trust: a free bootable image runs 8-hour retention, pattern and row-hammer tests on any host and signs the result with the module's SPD serial; ~$600k builds the software, signing service and three pilot broker integrations in 18 months.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in reuse; certified used DRAM sells at 40-60% of new and unlocks stranded DDR4 inventory.

title: One model per person: users as 1-bit deltas over shared base
idea: From the extreme of a personalized model for every user: each fine-tune is stored as a sign-only 1-bit delta mask with per-matrix scales over one resident base and applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel, so millions of personal models share a single base in HBM.
why: A 1-bit delta is 16x smaller than BF16 weights and is never materialized; per-user model memory falls 16x+, and water with it.

title: KV cache whose precision decays with token age and attention
idea: Box: approximate × KV manager × 16-token block × age-triggered × format ladder FP16→FP8→INT4→INT2→evict. A background re-quantizer demotes blocks as they age and as their accumulated attention mass stays low, while sink tokens and recently attended blocks stay at full precision.
why: Attention mass concentrates on recent and a few anchor tokens; an average of 3–4 bits per value instead of 16 shrinks long-context KV 4–5×.

title: Semantic snapshots: background apps keep only re-creatable state
idea: Imposed limit: a background phone app gets 2 MB. The OS makes each app serialize a semantic snapshot (navigation stack, form inputs, scroll positions, auth tokens) and then discards its heap; on relaunch the app rehydrates from the snapshot and a cached UI layout instead of restoring the whole heap.
why: Phones ship 12-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm; semantic snapshots could keep the same perceived warmth at 6-8 GB, and phones take roughly a third of all DRAM bits.
note: Android saved-instance-state already does this; adoption and perceived warmth are the hurdles.

title: OS lossy heap: applications declare error tolerance per allocation
idea: Inverts 'memory must be bit-exact': a new mmap flag (MAP_LOSSY plus an error bound) sends ML activations, image buffers and analytics sketches to a region where the memory controller applies error-bounded floating-point compression (ZFP/SZ-style) on writeback. Exactness stays the default; lossy bytes are opt-in and typed.
why: 3-8x effective capacity on tolerant data, which is often 30-60% of an ML or media server's footprint.

title: Retired GPUs become attention-computing KV-cache servers
idea: Combine previous-generation accelerators (HBM2-era parts on non-EUV processes) with attention offload: the new GPU ships query vectors over the network, the retired GPU holds long-context KV in its HBM and returns attention outputs, so only small vectors cross the link.
why: Turns stranded HBM2 into extra KV capacity without new DRAM and frees 50-70% of new GPUs' HBM for weights and batch.
